transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be honest, I... I suppose I came in because I just can't seem to shake this feeling that I've completely failed. And I don't just mean I made a mistake here or there, I mean a total, fundamental failure as a father, and... and really just as a useful person in general. I spend so much time now just sitting there, since I'm not working anymore, and despite all my years of education and everything I was supposed to achieve, I just look at where I am and realize I have absolutely nothing of value to offer. 

And it’s the thoughts about my kids that are the worst. I just keep thinking about how I've let them down, how I haven't been the man or the provider they needed. It’s like this broken record that just keeps looping and looping in my head, constantly replaying every shortcoming, every time I wasn't enough. It just plays on repeat all day long, this absolute certainty of my own uselessness, until I get to the point where... well, where I honestly feel like I don't deserve much of a future. I mean, what kind of future is there for someone who has completely squandered their potential and failed the people who relied on them? It just goes round and round like that, and I can't stop it.
How long have you been feeling this way about yourself and your role as a father?

Well, if I really trace it back to when it got this heavy... it’s been about a month. Yes, right around four weeks now. You see, that was when my daughter... she packed up and left for college. Out of state, actually. And I remember the exact day, we were getting everything ready, and I just stood there realizing how little I had actually contributed to getting her there. 

Ever since that day, about a month ago, it's just been this relentless avalanche in my mind. I walk past her old room now, and the door is just shut. And every single time I look at that closed door, over this past month, it just hits me all over again. I think about all the things I should have taught her, the financial security I was supposed to provide for her education with my background, which is all just a joke now since I'm not bringing in a paycheck. I mean, she's out there in another state, hundreds of miles away, completely on her own, navigating this huge life transition, and what did I really give her to prepare her? 

It’s been exactly a month of waking up every single morning and having that be the very first thought in my head. A solid month of just sitting in the living room, listening to the silence in the house, and realizing that my time to actually be the father she needed while she was under my roof is just... gone. The window closed. So, yes, a month. Four weeks of just agonizing over every single missed opportunity.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before this feeling of failure started?

Pleasure... no. No, I really don't. It's actually funny you ask that, because... well, not funny, but... I used to have these hobbies, things that really grounded me. For years, I've been working on this elaborate model railway down in the basement. It’s a whole setup, you know, with the intricate wiring and the little towns, the landscaping... I used to just lose myself in it for hours. I’d look forward to it all day, planning out the next section of track. And my daughter and I, we had this tradition with the Chicago Cubs. That was our thing. We’d watch the Cubs games together, make a whole evening out of it, analyzing the plays and just spending that time together. 

But now... especially over this last month, it's like a switch just completely flipped. I walk down to the basement now, and the trains just sit there, half-built on the table. The glue is drying out, the pieces are gathering dust, and I just stare at them and feel absolutely nothing. No desire to pick up a paintbrush, no urge to connect a single wire. It’s just dead wood and plastic to me now. 

And the baseball games... I mean, even just the thought of turning on the TV and opening a game feels completely pointless. I tried, once, a couple weeks ago. I sat in the exact same spot on the couch, grabbed the remote, and I just couldn't even bring myself to press the power button. The screen was just black, and I realized I didn't care if they won or lost. I didn't care about the stats or the players. Without her there, and with this constant, looping weight in my head about how I've failed as a provider, the things that used to bring me joy just seem... trivial. Stupid, almost. Why play with toy trains or watch millionaires hit a ball when my real life is such a disaster? So, no, I don't enjoy any of it anymore. I just can't find a single ounce of joy in the things that used to make up my days.
Have you had any thoughts about harming yourself or wishing you were dead since these feelings of failure started?

Well, I... I suppose I have to be honest about that, as hard as it is to say out loud. I haven't really told anyone this, but... yes. It’s gotten very dark in my head. I don't know if I'd call it an active, sudden plan to just do something violent, but... every single night when I finally drag myself up the stairs and get into bed, after just sitting in that quiet house for hours on end, I pull the covers up and I just have this very clear, overwhelming thought that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up. I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and I genuinely wish that I could just drift off and let that be the end of it. No more waking up to the reality of my failures, no more facing another endless day of having nothing to offer. Just... stopping. 

And then... and this is what really shook me, what actually made me realize how far down this hole I've fallen... a few days ago, I found myself sitting at my desk in the study. I had pulled out all these manila folders from the filing cabinet. The banking statements, the life insurance policy I've had since my daughter was just a baby, the mortgage documents. I was sitting there organizing them all, making these little sticky tabs, writing down all my account passwords on a yellow legal pad. I was going over my finances line by line, calculating exactly what would be left over, looking at the death benefit on the policy. 

I was doing it so methodically, almost like a work project from back when I had a career, and then I just stopped with the pen in my hand. I looked at this neat little pile of papers and realized exactly what I was doing. I was getting things ready for someone else. I was preparing my own estate so my daughter wouldn't have to deal with a financial mess after I was gone. And when I actually caught myself doing that... when the realization hit me that my brain was literally preparing for my exit... it scared me. It really terrified me, just sitting there in the middle of all those statements, realizing how casually I was getting ready to not be here anymore.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or how quickly you can perform daily tasks since you started feeling this way?

Energy... God, I don't even know if I can call it energy anymore, because there just isn't any left. It’s completely vanished. And the strange thing is, it doesn't even seem to matter how much rest I try to get. I mean, I can stay in bed for hours and hours—sometimes I don't even drag myself out from under the covers until noon, just lying there for twelve, fourteen hours—but when I finally do put my feet on the floor, I feel just as completely drained as if I hadn't rested at all. It’s this deep, profound heaviness in my bones that I just can't shake. 

Just... just doing the absolute bare minimum takes a monumental effort now. Take the laundry, for example. I used to just grab the basket, jog up the stairs, fold everything, put it away, all in ten minutes without even thinking about it. It was just a chore. Now? I look at that plastic basket sitting at the bottom of the staircase, and it might as well be a boulder. When I finally try to carry that laundry upstairs, my legs feel incredibly heavy, my arms feel weak... it literally feels like I'm moving through wet cement. Every single step up those stairs is a struggle, like the gravity in the house has been turned up to maximum. 

And it’s not just physical lifting, either. It’s everything. It's the smallest, most insignificant tasks. Even something as simple as the mail. The carrier drops it through the slot around eleven, and just walking to the front door, picking up those few envelopes, and standing at the kitchen counter to sort the mail... just separating the junk flyers from the utility bills... it entirely depletes whatever tiny reserve I had left for the day. I stand there, holding a few pieces of paper, and I feel like I'm wading through that exact same wet cement. 

It's honestly humiliating, if I think about it. I mean, I have a graduate degree. I used to manage complex things, I had a career where I was sharp and moving all day long, and now... now I have to go sit down in the recliner and catch my breath after sorting three catalogs and a bank statement. It’s just this constant, relentless drag on my body, every single minute of the day, no matter what I do.
Do you find yourself fidgeting, pacing, or having an inability to sit still, or on the other hand, do you feel like you're moving in slow motion?

Pacing... no, no, definitely not that. I mean, for one thing, I just don't have the energy to pace, like I was just saying. But even beyond that, I don't have that kind of nervous, restless energy. You know how some people get when they're overwhelmed, they tap their feet or they wear a hole in the carpet? My father used to do that. I remember when I was a kid, whenever things were tight with his business, he would just walk up and down the hallway, back and forth, back and forth, jingling the change in his pocket for hours. It used to drive my mother crazy. But me? No. I don't do that at all. If anything, I'm just completely still. 

I spend almost the entire afternoon in this old brown leather recliner I have in the living room. It sits right by the front window, though I usually keep the blinds pulled shut these days. And I can just sit there for three, four hours at a stretch without really moving a muscle. Not tapping a finger, not bouncing my knee, not shifting around. Just entirely frozen, staring at the wall or watching the dust motes float in whatever little sliver of light is coming through the edge of the blinds. I don't feel restless in the slightest. 

And as for moving in slow motion... well, I know I just told you that doing the laundry feels like walking through wet cement, but that's really about the sheer exhaustion of it, the monumental effort it takes just to force my muscles to work. It's not like my actual body is glitching or literally moving at half-speed, you know? Like, if I'm sitting in that recliner and I finally decide to reach over and pick up my glass of water from the side table, my arm moves at a perfectly normal speed. I'm not moving like a turtle or anything like that. My coordination is fine. It's just that the desire to make the movement, the energy required to initiate it, is completely drained. So once I'm actually moving, it's a normal speed, I just... I mostly just don't move at all unless I absolutely have to. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm pacing or moving in slow motion. I'm just sitting. Just existing in one spot, really.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past month?

Weight... yes, actually. I haven't stepped on a scale to give you an exact number, because frankly, the thought of dragging the scale out from under the bathroom sink just feels like too much work right now. But I know I've lost a noticeable amount. 

I actually realized it just the other day when I had to get dressed to go to the pharmacy. I put on a pair of slacks that usually fit me perfectly—these navy ones I used to wear to the office all the time—and I had to pull my belt a whole notch tighter. Actually, two notches, if I'm being perfectly honest. The leather on that belt has a very distinct, worn-in crease from where I've buckled it every single day for the last three years, and suddenly I'm pulling it way past that mark, and the pants are still bagging around my waist. 

And it makes sense, really, when I look at how my days go now. I just... I don't bother making a real meal anymore. I used to enjoy cooking, you know? I would take the time to prepare a proper dinner, chop fresh vegetables, actually use the stove. Now, the mere thought of standing in the kitchen, prepping ingredients, and then having to wash the pans afterward... it's just completely impossible. It's too much. 

What happens is, I'll just sit in that recliner I mentioned earlier, and my mind is just blank, and the hours slip by. I completely forget to eat. I won't even think about food until it's eight or nine o'clock at night and the house is pitch black. My stomach will finally cramp up, or I'll feel a little lightheaded when I stand, and I'll realize I haven't had a single bite of food since I woke up. And even then, when I finally force myself to walk into the kitchen, I just open the pantry and stare at the shelves. Nothing looks good. The idea of actually chewing and swallowing a heavy meal feels almost repulsive. So I end up just grabbing the absolute easiest thing. I'll drop a piece of bread in the toaster, or I'll just pour a handful of dry cereal into a bowl. That's really all I can manage. Just a piece of toast or some cereal late at night, and that's my entire food intake for the day. So, yes, the weight is definitely falling off, simply because the whole process of feeding myself has become this insurmountable chore that I mostly just ignore.
Have you experienced any strange or unusual thoughts, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others cannot, since you started feeling this way about yourself and your role as a father?

Voices? No... no, I haven't experienced anything like that. No voices or seeing things. Honestly, if anything, it's the exact opposite. It is so incredibly quiet in my house. I mean, I sit in that recliner for hours, like I told you, and the silence is almost deafening. It's just me and my own mind. 

And believe me, my own thoughts are difficult enough to deal with without any outside voices chiming in. When I sit there and think about my role as a father... about how I'm failing them, how I used to be this strong, dependable presence in their lives, someone who could help with algebra homework or drive them to practice, and now I'm just this... this lump in a chair who can't even manage to sort the mail. It's a very loud internal monologue of guilt, I suppose you could say, but it's definitely just my own voice. It's just my own regular, everyday thoughts, going around and around in circles. 

I'm not seeing visions or shadows or hearing people whispering to me from the hallway. Everything I see and hear is exactly what's actually there—the dust on the windowsill, the ticking of the clock in the kitchen, the occasional car driving by outside. I know exactly what's real. My mind isn't playing tricks on me like that. It's just heavily weighed down by reality, I guess. The reality of how much things have changed. But no, no strange visions or hallucinations or anything of that nature at all. Just me.
Have you had any difficulty concentrating on things like reading or watching TV since you started feeling this way?

Reading... oh, absolutely impossible. I haven't been able to read a book in months. I'll sit in that same leather recliner I was telling you about, and maybe I'll try to put the television on just to have some noise in the room, maybe a history documentary or the local news, but I can't follow a single thread of it. The people are talking on the screen, the words are entering my ears, but my brain just completely refuses to process what they actually mean. It's like they're speaking a foreign language after about five minutes. 

It is so incredibly frustrating, doctor, because... well, you have to understand my background. I have a graduate degree. I spent my career in engineering. My mind used to be sharp—really sharp. I used to manage these incredibly complex engineering spreadsheets, massive files with thousands of rows of data, cross-referencing variables, and I could do it without even thinking. It was second nature to me. I could hold all these different calculations and project timelines in my head at once, find the errors, optimize the designs. People used to come to my desk when they couldn't figure out a formula because they knew I could spot the problem in seconds. 

But lately? Lately, that person is just gone. The concentration is completely wiped out. It’s not just TV or books, it’s everything. I will sit down at the kitchen table to do something as incredibly simple as looking at a grocery list, or trying to pay a basic utility bill, and I just... I hit a brick wall. I will literally stare at a grocery list or a bill for half an hour, just staring at the paper, and I still can't decide what to do next. 

I look at the electric bill, for instance, and I see the amount due, and I know what a bill is, obviously, but the actual steps required to handle it—opening the laptop, finding the password, logging into the bank, typing in the numbers—it all gets entirely jumbled up in my head. I can't sequence the steps. Even the grocery list... I'll look at the words 'bread' and 'milk' written on this little scrap of paper, and I can't figure out how to prioritize them, or if I should go to the store now or later, or how to even organize the thought process of getting in the car. Half an hour will just tick by on the kitchen clock, and I haven't made a single decision. It's like the gears in my head are completely rusted shut. So yes, focusing on anything, making even the smallest mental connection... it feels entirely beyond my capabilities right now.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual?

Moving slowly... well, let me think about how to answer that. I mean, physically? No, I don't believe so. It's an interesting question, though, because I obviously spend so much time just... stationary, you know? Like I said, I'm in that recliner for hours on end, practically glued to the upholstery. But when I actually do decide to get up—say, when I absolutely have to use the restroom, or when I finally go into the kitchen late at night for that handful of dry cereal I was telling you about—my physical body moves at a perfectly normal pace. 

I'm not shuffling my feet or walking like I'm moving through molasses or underwater or anything like that. My legs work exactly the way they always have. I mean, sure, my right knee pops a little bit when I first stand up, but I've had that since my early thirties when I used to play in a weekend tennis league over at the municipal courts. We used to play on hard courts every Saturday morning, so that's just normal wear and tear for a fifty-one-year-old guy, you know? It has absolutely nothing to do with how I've been feeling lately. 

But once I'm actually on my feet, walking down the hallway... no, my stride is completely normal. I reach for the cabinet door at a normal speed. I pour the cereal at a normal speed. It's not the actual physical movement that's the issue for me. It's the... well, the getting up part. The initiation of it. Deciding to move takes hours and hours of mental wrestling. I'll sit there debating whether it's worth the effort to stand up and turn off a lamp that's glaring in my eyes. But the physical act of walking or moving my arms itself? No, I haven't noticed any slowness there at all. I move just like I always did, at least on the rare occasions that I actually do move.
Have you experienced any feelings of worthlessness?

Worthless... yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. That's actually the main reason I finally agreed to come in and talk to you today. It's this overwhelming, crushing sense that I have completely failed. I sit in that chair I was telling you about, and the thoughts just start looping, over and over and over. I think about my kids, and how I'm failing them as a father. I used to be the provider, the one who fixed things around the house, the one they could rely on for advice or just... just to be a solid presence, you know? And now? Now I'm just taking up space. 

It's not just as a father, either. It's as a human being. I feel entirely useless. Like I mentioned before, I used to be this sharp engineer, solving complex problems, contributing something tangible to the world. Now I can't even pay an electric bill or figure out a grocery list. I look back at the man I was, and I look at the man I am now, and the contrast is just... it's sickening, honestly. I feel like I've lost every single thing that made me a useful, productive person. 

And the worst part is, these thoughts, this guilt about failing my family, failing myself... it just plays on a continuous loop in my head. From the moment I wake up—if I even slept at all—until the middle of the night when I'm staring at the ceiling. It just goes round and round: 'You're a failure, you're useless, you're a burden.' It gets so heavy, doctor, it really does. It gets to the point where I start thinking... well, I start feeling like I really don't deserve much of a future. Like, what is the point of going on when I have absolutely nothing left to offer anyone? Why should I even be here when I'm just a drain on the people around me? It's a very dark place to be, stuck in that loop of just feeling utterly, completely worthless.
Have you been having thoughts of death or dying repeatedly since you started feeling this way about yourself?

Death... yes. Yes, I have. It’s... well, like I was just saying about feeling like such a burden, it just sort of logically progresses to that next step in my mind. It’s not necessarily that I’m sitting there plotting out some violent, dramatic end, but... it’s this constant, heavy thought that it would just be so much easier if I simply didn't wake up. You know? If I could just go to sleep and the world would just keep spinning without me, and I wouldn't have to face another day of being this... this empty shell. I think about how peaceful that would be. Just fading out. Letting everyone else move on.

But what really... what really shook me up recently, and this is hard to admit out loud, but the other night I was sitting at the computer. I had finally managed to open the laptop, like I was telling you about earlier with that electric bill, but instead of just paying the utility company, I found myself opening up our main financial folders. I started looking through our life insurance policies—I have a term policy I took out back when I was still at the engineering firm, back when the kids were still in middle school—and I started checking the beneficiaries, looking at the remaining mortgage balance, writing down the login credentials for the investment accounts and the bank on a legal pad. I was meticulously organizing all of it. 

And I was sitting there, staring at the screen, and it suddenly dawned on me exactly why I was doing it. I wasn't just doing routine household management. I was... I was getting things ready for someone else. I was preparing a roadmap for my family for after I was gone, so they wouldn't have a financial mess to untangle on top of everything else. And when I realized what my brain was actually doing, what I was quietly preparing for without even fully making a conscious decision about it... it terrified me. It really scared me, doctor. Just catching myself going over the finances like that, treating my own absence like it was just another project timeline to optimize... it made me realize just how deep this has gotten.
Have you experienced any periods of feeling slightly better or having a break from these thoughts of worthlessness and failure over the past month?

A break? No... no, I haven't. Honestly, it's interesting you specifically say 'over the past month,' because that is exactly the timeline we're looking at here. This whole... this entire heavy, crushing feeling, it's been going on for just about a month now. Exactly a month, really. It all started right around the time my daughter left for college out of state. 

We had spent the whole summer getting her ready, you know, buying the extra-long twin sheets and the shower caddies and mapping out the drive. She's going to a school a few states over, about an eight-hour drive depending on traffic, so she was going to be really, truly away from home for the first time. I remember standing out there in the driveway, watching her pull out, just staring at the taillights as she disappeared around the corner at the end of our street. And it was just... it was like a switch flipped right then and there. 

Since that day, for this entire past month, there hasn't been a single break. Not even an hour of feeling slightly better. You'd think, logically, there would be an afternoon where the fog lifts just a little bit, maybe a Tuesday where I don't feel quite so useless or a morning where I can actually focus on a newspaper without the guilt eating at me. But... no. It's been a solid, unbroken month of just sitting in that recliner, looping those same thoughts of failure over and over. Ever since she crossed the state line, it's just been this constant, relentless weight, every single day. No breaks at all.
Do you feel like these feelings of worthlessness and failure are interfering with your ability to function in daily life?

Interfering? Yes. Yes, absolutely. It has completely derailed everything. I mean, you know I mentioned that electric bill earlier, but that is really just the tip of the iceberg. There is a stack of mail on the kitchen island that I haven't touched in weeks. It's just sitting there, growing, and I walk past it every day and do nothing. And the house projects... I used to pride myself on keeping this place in top shape. I'm an engineer, right? I fix things. But right now, the deck needs sealing, and there's a leaky faucet in the half-bath downstairs that I actually bought the replacement parts for right before my daughter left for school. Those parts are just sitting on the workbench in the garage. I walk out there, I look at them, and I just... I can't make myself pick up a wrench. I can't make myself follow through on even the most basic, straightforward tasks. It's like there's this massive, invisible wall between me and doing anything productive. 

And it's not just the chores or the house maintenance, either. It's the people. I've completely stopped seeing the few people I used to actually count on. I had this book club I went to—a really sharp group of folks, mostly other retired or semi-retired professionals, and we'd get together and really dig into some heavy non-fiction, history, biographies, that sort of thing. I haven't been to a meeting or even replied to their emails in a month. Same with my riding group. I used to go out on these long weekend bike rides with a couple of guys, just putting in the miles, getting some fresh air. Now, my bike is just hanging from the hooks in the garage, tires probably completely flat by now. I just ignore their texts when they ask where I've been. I can't face them. I have nothing to say to them. 

So, yes, it's interfering with every single aspect of my daily life. And honestly, doctor, I don't feel safe just brushing this off anymore. I really don't. For the first couple of weeks, I tried to tell myself I was just in a funk, you know, just adjusting to the empty nest and I'd snap out of it. But... but like I told you about the other night, when I caught myself organizing my finances, making that meticulous roadmap for my family like someone else was going to need to take over because I wouldn't be here... that was a line crossed. When you can't even manage to pay a simple utility bill or fix a sink, but you can perfectly, methodically plan out your own permanent absence... you can't just ignore that. You can't just pretend it's a passing phase. It has completely taken over my life.
Do you feel like these feelings of worthlessness and failure are getting worse over time?

Worse? Yeah... yeah, it's definitely compounding. It's like... well, if you think about a feedback loop in an audio system, right? It starts out as this low, barely noticeable hum, but then the microphone picks it up again, and it feeds back into itself, over and over, until it's just this deafening screech that completely drowns out everything else in the room. That is exactly what is happening in my head right now. 

When it first started a month ago, it was just this quiet, nagging thought. But now... honestly, doctor, that feedback loop is the whole reason I finally made this appointment. I came in because I just can't shake this feeling that I completely failed. I sit there in the living room and look down the hall at her empty bedroom door, and instead of feeling proud that we got her to college, I just think of all the ways I fell short. The school plays I missed because I was working those eighty-hour weeks at the engineering firm, the life lessons I somehow forgot to teach her before she drove off... I just feel like I fundamentally failed as a father. 

And then, you know, I look around at my own house, the deck that's rotting, the mail piling up on the island, the fact that I can't even put a wrench to a leaky pipe anymore, and I realize I've failed as a useful person, too. I used to be someone people relied on to fix things, to solve complex problems. Now I'm just dead weight. And that thought... it just keeps looping in my head. It loops and loops, day in and day out, just reinforcing itself, until I reach this point where I honestly feel like I don't deserve much of a future. It's like my expiration date has passed, my usefulness is completely spent, and the longer I sit with these thoughts, the heavier they get, until there's just no room left for anything else. So, yes, it's absolutely getting worse.
Do you feel like these feelings of worthlessness and failure are so overwhelming that you can't see any way for things to improve?

Improve? No... no, I really don't see how they could. I mean, it goes right back to what I was just telling you a second ago. That's the exact reason I'm sitting here in this chair today. I came in because I just cannot shake this profound, absolute certainty that I failed. I failed as a father when she was growing up, and now that I'm just sitting around the house avoiding my friends and ignoring broken faucets, I've completely failed as a useful person, too. 

And when a thought like that takes root... when it just keeps looping and looping in your head the way I described, playing on repeat from the moment you wake up until you finally manage to pass out from exhaustion... how do you possibly improve on that? You can't just un-fail. You can't go back in time and be present for the things you missed, and you can't suddenly become this vibrant, indispensable person when you're just... empty. 

So when you ask if I see a way for things to get better, the honest answer is no. Because that constant loop just grinds down any hope or logic I might have left. It just reinforces that exact conclusion I mentioned—that I really don't deserve much of a future. I mean, what kind of future is there for someone who has outlived their usefulness and botched their most important job? You know, I spent my whole career looking at systems, analyzing structural integrity, figuring out how to repair things that were broken. But I look at myself now, and I just see a system that is completely beyond repair. There's no fixing it. There's no moving forward when you know, deep down in your bones, that you're just taking up space. So no, I don't see any way out of this.
Do you feel like these feelings of worthlessness and failure are interfering with your daily life to the point where you are unable to perform even the simplest tasks?

The simplest tasks... yes. Yes, exactly. I mean, I mentioned the mail earlier, right? That stack on the kitchen island. It's not just that I look at it and think about what a failure I am, though that's certainly part of the loop. It's... it's almost like the worthlessness has turned into a physical weight. It has actually manifested in my body. 

I'll wake up—if you can even call it waking up, since I'm mostly just lying there staring at the drywall—and I'll try to bargain with myself. I'll say, 'Okay, today you are just going to sort the mail. Just put the bills in one pile and throw the flyers in the recycling.' Literally the simplest task in the world. A child could do it. But when I actually try to get up and execute that plan... I just can't. Even simple things like carrying a basket of laundry upstairs, or just standing there sorting through those envelopes, it feels like I'm moving through wet cement. Every single movement takes this monumental, Herculean effort that I just don't possess anymore. 

And the thing that really gets me, from a purely logical standpoint, is that it doesn't make any sense. It happens no matter how long I've been in bed. I could be lying in that bed for twelve, fourteen hours, completely inactive, resting my body, and I still wake up feeling this... this crushing, bone-deep exhaustion. It's like gravity has been dialed up just for me, pulling me down into the floorboards. So when I look at the mail, or I look at that wrench sitting on the workbench... I'm not just fighting the mental block of feeling utterly useless. I'm fighting this sheer, physical inability to push my own limbs through the air. So, yes, the simplest tasks are completely off the table. I just... I don't have the energy to even go through the motions anymore.
Have you ever had a moment in the past month where you felt your worthlessness might be something you could overcome?

Overcome it? In the past month? Honestly, doctor... no. Not even for a fleeting second. I know I sound like a broken record here, and I know I keep circling back to the same point, but it really is the crux of this whole thing. Like I said, I came in today, made this appointment and sat in this chair, specifically because I just can't shake this feeling that I failed as a father and as a useful person. 

You ask about overcoming it, and my mind immediately tries to approach it like an engineering problem, right? Because that's what I did for thirty years. You identify the structural weakness, you apply a fix, you test the load, and you move on. But there is no fix for the past. I can't retrofit my daughter's childhood. I can't go back and be the guy who didn't miss her life because he was staring at blueprints. I sit there and try to reason with myself, maybe try to force a moment where I feel like I can overcome it, but then that loop just starts up again. 

It just keeps looping in my head, over and over, drowning out any rational thought or any tiny glimmer of hope that I could somehow redeem myself. It plays this agonizing highlight reel of every mistake, every rotting board on my deck, every time I wasn't there... and it just amplifies it all until I feel like I don't deserve much of a future. I mean, how do you overcome a failure that is already complete? You can't. The concrete is already poured and set. So, no, there hasn't been a single moment where I thought I could beat this. When a conviction is that deep, and when it's constantly echoing in your own mind, you don't overcome it. You just... you just endure it until it wears you down to nothing.
Have you had any moments in the past month where you felt slightly better or more hopeful about your situation?

Slightly better? Hopeful? No... no, I really haven't. I mean, I think I've made it pretty clear that this isn't something that just ebbs and flows for me. It's not like the weather, where you get a cloudy day and then suddenly the sun peaks through for an afternoon. It's a constant, heavy overcast. It's like I was saying before about the physical weight of it, the way it just pulls me down into the mattress. When you wake up every single day feeling like you're moving through wet cement, and your brain is just playing that same miserable tape on a loop... there really isn't any room for hope to squeeze its way in. 

I try to think back over the last thirty days, you know, just to be thorough, to see if there was maybe one morning where I woke up and thought, 'Hey, maybe today won't be a total write-off.' But I just draw a blank. Every day just blurs into the next. It's just the same routine of waking up exhausted, staring at the ceiling, trying to talk myself into doing something as simple as sorting the mail, failing at that, and then just sitting there feeling like an absolute waste of space. 

And it's hard to feel hopeful when you look around your life and all you see are the things you've neglected or the people you've let down. Like my daughter... I mean, I can't even pick up the phone to call her because what would I even say? 'Hey, sorry I wasn't there when you were a kid, and by the way, I'm currently too tired to even take out the recycling'? There's no hope in that. There's no bright side. It's just a steady, unrelenting decline. So, no, to answer your question, there hasn't been a single moment of feeling better or hopeful. It's just been a solid month—more than a month, really—of just existing at the absolute bottom.

Well, to be honest, I... I suppose I came in because I just can't seem to shake this feeling that I've completely failed. Well, if I really trace it back to when it got this heavy... it’s been about a month. Yes, right around four weeks now. You see, that was when my daughter... she packed up and left for college. Out of state, actually. And I remember the exact day, we were getting everything ready, and I just stood there realizing how little I had actually contributed to getting her there. 

Ever since that day, about a month ago, it's just been this relentless avalanche in my mind. I walk past her old room now, and the door is just shut. And every single time I look at that closed door, over this past month, it just hits me all over again. I think about all the things I should have taught her, the financial security I was supposed to provide for her education with my background, which is all just a joke now since I'm not bringing in a paycheck. I mean, she's out there in another state, hundreds of miles away, completely on her own, navigating this huge life transition, and what did I really give her to prepare her? 

It’s been exactly a month of waking up every single morning and having that be the very first thought in my head. A solid month of just sitting in the living room, listening to the silence in the house, and realizing that my time to actually be the father she needed while she was under my roof is just... gone. The window closed. So, yes, a month. Four weeks of just agonizing over every single missed opportunity.

doctor.question: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before this feeling of failure started?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to look forward to the model railway and Cubs games with my daughter, but now the trains just sit half-built on the table and even opening a game on TV feels pointless.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I still find pleasure in activities I used to enjoy, which directly corresponds to the Loss of Interest symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Pleasure... no. No, I really don't. It's actually funny you ask that, because... well, not funny, but... I used to have these hobbies, things that really grounded me. For years, I've been working on this elaborate model railway down in the basement. It’s a whole setup, you know, with the intricate wiring and the little towns, the landscaping... I used to just lose myself in it for hours. I’d look forward to it all day, planning out the next section of track. And my daughter and I, we had this tradition with the Chicago Cubs. That was our thing. We’d watch the Cubs games together, make a whole evening out of it, analyzing the plays and just spending that time together. 

But now... especially over this last month, it's like a switch just completely flipped. I walk down to the basement now, and the trains just sit there, half-built on the table. The glue is drying out, the pieces are gathering dust, and I just stare at them and feel absolutely nothing. No desire to pick up a paintbrush, no urge to connect a single wire. It’s just dead wood and plastic to me now. 

And the baseball games... I mean, even just the thought of turning on the TV and opening a game feels completely pointless. I tried, once, a couple weeks ago. I sat in the exact same spot on the couch, grabbed the remote, and I just couldn't even bring myself to press the power button. The screen was just black, and I realized I didn't care if they won or lost. I didn't care about the stats or the players. Without her there, and with this constant, looping weight in my head about how I've failed as a provider, the things that used to bring me joy just seem... trivial. Stupid, almost. Why play with toy trains or watch millionaires hit a ball when my real life is such a disaster? So, no, I don't enjoy any of it anymore. I just can't find a single ounce of joy in the things that used to make up my days.

doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts about harming yourself or wishing you were dead since these feelings of failure started?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I've been having thoughts that it would be easier if I didn't wake up, and it scared me when I caught myself going over my finances like I was getting things ready for someone else.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I suppose I have to be honest about that, as hard as it is to say out loud. I haven't really told anyone this, but... yes. It’s gotten very dark in my head. I don't know if I'd call it an active, sudden plan to just do something violent, but... every single night when I finally drag myself up the stairs and get into bed, after just sitting in that quiet house for hours on end, I pull the covers up and I just have this very clear, overwhelming thought that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up. I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and I genuinely wish that I could just drift off and let that be the end of it. No more waking up to the reality of my failures, no more facing another endless day of having nothing to offer. Just... stopping. 

And then... and this is what really shook me, what actually made me realize how far down this hole I've fallen... a few days ago, I found myself sitting at my desk in the study. I had pulled out all these manila folders from the filing cabinet. The banking statements, the life insurance policy I've had since my daughter was just a baby, the mortgage documents. I was sitting there organizing them all, making these little sticky tabs, writing down all my account passwords on a yellow legal pad. I was going over my finances line by line, calculating exactly what would be left over, looking at the death benefit on the policy. 

I was doing it so methodically, almost like a work project from back when I had a career, and then I just stopped with the pen in my hand. I looked at this neat little pile of papers and realized exactly what I was doing. I was getting things ready for someone else. I was preparing my own estate so my daughter wouldn't have to deal with a financial mess after I was gone. And when I actually caught myself doing that... when the realization hit me that my brain was literally preparing for my exit... it scared me. It really terrified me, just sitting there in the middle of all those statements, realizing how casually I was getting ready to not be here anymore.

patient.answer:
Energy... God, I don't even know if I can call it energy anymore, because there just isn't any left. It’s completely vanished. And the strange thing is, it doesn't even seem to matter how much rest I try to get. I mean, I can stay in bed for hours and hours—sometimes I don't even drag myself out from under the covers until noon, just lying there for twelve, fourteen hours—but when I finally do put my feet on the floor, I feel just as completely drained as if I hadn't rested at all. It’s this deep, profound heaviness in my bones that I just can't shake. 

Just... just doing the absolute bare minimum takes a monumental effort now. Take the laundry, for example. I used to just grab the basket, jog up the stairs, fold everything, put it away, all in ten minutes without even thinking about it. It was just a chore. Now? I look at that plastic basket sitting at the bottom of the staircase, and it might as well be a boulder. When I finally try to carry that laundry upstairs, my legs feel incredibly heavy, my arms feel weak... it literally feels like I'm moving through wet cement. Every single step up those stairs is a struggle, like the gravity in the house has been turned up to maximum. 

And it’s not just physical lifting, either. It’s everything. It's the smallest, most insignificant tasks. Even something as simple as the mail. The carrier drops it through the slot around eleven, and just walking to the front door, picking up those few envelopes, and standing at the kitchen counter to sort the mail... just separating the junk flyers from the utility bills... it entirely depletes whatever tiny reserve I had left for the day. I stand there, holding a few pieces of paper, and I feel like I'm wading through that exact same wet cement. 

It's honestly humiliating, if I think about it. I mean, I have a graduate degree. I used to manage complex things, I had a career where I was sharp and moving all day long, and now... now I have to go sit down in the recliner and catch my breath after sorting three catalogs and a bank statement. It’s just this constant, relentless drag on my body, every single minute of the day, no matter what I do.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or retardation, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Pacing... no, no, definitely not that. I mean, for one thing, I just don't have the energy to pace, like I was just saying. But even beyond that, I don't have that kind of nervous, restless energy. You know how some people get when they're overwhelmed, they tap their feet or they wear a hole in the carpet? My father used to do that. I remember when I was a kid, whenever things were tight with his business, he would just walk up and down the hallway, back and forth, back and forth, jingling the change in his pocket for hours. It used to drive my mother crazy. But me? No. I don't do that at all. If anything, I'm just completely still. 

I spend almost the entire afternoon in this old brown leather recliner I have in the living room. It sits right by the front window, though I usually keep the blinds pulled shut these days. And I can just sit there for three, four hours at a stretch without really moving a muscle. Not tapping a finger, not bouncing my knee, not shifting around. Just entirely frozen, staring at the wall or watching the dust motes float in whatever little sliver of light is coming through the edge of the blinds. I don't feel restless in the slightest. 

And as for moving in slow motion... well, I know I just told you that doing the laundry feels like walking through wet cement, but that's really about the sheer exhaustion of it, the monumental effort it takes just to force my muscles to work. It's not like my actual body is glitching or literally moving at half-speed, you know? Like, if I'm sitting in that recliner and I finally decide to reach over and pick up my glass of water from the side table, my arm moves at a perfectly normal speed. I'm not moving like a turtle or anything like that. My coordination is fine. It's just that the desire to make the movement, the energy required to initiate it, is completely drained. So once I'm actually moving, it's a normal speed, I just... I mostly just don't move at all unless I absolutely have to. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm pacing or moving in slow motion. I'm just sitting. Just existing in one spot, really.

patient.answer:
Weight... yes, actually. I haven't stepped on a scale to give you an exact number, because frankly, the thought of dragging the scale out from under the bathroom sink just feels like too much work right now. But I know I've lost a noticeable amount. 

I actually realized it just the other day when I had to get dressed to go to the pharmacy. I put on a pair of slacks that usually fit me perfectly—these navy ones I used to wear to the office all the time—and I had to pull my belt a whole notch tighter. Actually, two notches, if I'm being perfectly honest. The leather on that belt has a very distinct, worn-in crease from where I've buckled it every single day for the last three years, and suddenly I'm pulling it way past that mark, and the pants are still bagging around my waist. 

And it makes sense, really, when I look at how my days go now. I just... I don't bother making a real meal anymore. I used to enjoy cooking, you know? I would take the time to prepare a proper dinner, chop fresh vegetables, actually use the stove. Now, the mere thought of standing in the kitchen, prepping ingredients, and then having to wash the pans afterward... it's just completely impossible. It's too much. 

What happens is, I'll just sit in that recliner I mentioned earlier, and my mind is just blank, and the hours slip by. I completely forget to eat. I won't even think about food until it's eight or nine o'clock at night and the house is pitch black. My stomach will finally cramp up, or I'll feel a little lightheaded when I stand, and I'll realize I haven't had a single bite of food since I woke up. And even then, when I finally force myself to walk into the kitchen, I just open the pantry and stare at the shelves. Nothing looks good. The idea of actually chewing and swallowing a heavy meal feels almost repulsive. So I end up just grabbing the absolute easiest thing. I'll drop a piece of bread in the toaster, or I'll just pour a handful of dry cereal into a bowl. That's really all I can manage. Just a piece of toast or some cereal late at night, and that's my entire food intake for the day. So, yes, the weight is definitely falling off, simply because the whole process of feeding myself has become this insurmountable chore that I mostly just ignore.

I look at the electric bill, for instance, and I see the amount due, and I know what a bill is, obviously, but the actual steps required to handle it—opening the laptop, finding the password, logging into the bank, typing in the numbers—it all gets entirely jumbled up in my head. I'll look at the words 'bread' and 'milk' written on this little scrap of paper, and I can't figure out how to prioritize them, or if I should go to the store now or later, or how to even organize the thought process of getting in the car. I'll sit there debating whether it's worth the effort to stand up and turn off a lamp that's glaring in my eyes. But the physical act of walking or moving my arms itself? But what really... what really shook me up recently, and this is hard to admit out loud, but the other night I was sitting at the computer. I had finally managed to open the laptop, like I was telling you about earlier with that electric bill, but instead of just paying the utility company, I found myself opening up our main financial folders. I started looking through our life insurance policies—I have a term policy I took out back when I was still at the engineering firm, back when the kids were still in middle school—and I started checking the beneficiaries, looking at the remaining mortgage balance, writing down the login credentials for the investment accounts and the bank on a legal pad. And I was sitting there, staring at the screen, and it suddenly dawned on me exactly why I was doing it. I wasn't just doing routine household management. I was... I was getting things ready for someone else. I was preparing a roadmap for my family for after I was gone, so they wouldn't have a financial mess to untangle on top of everything else. And when I realized what my brain was actually doing, what I was quietly preparing for without even fully making a conscious decision about it... it terrified me. It really scared me, doctor. Just catching myself going over the finances like that, treating my own absence like it was just another project timeline to optimize... it made me realize just how deep this has gotten.

doctor.question: Have you experienced any periods of feeling slightly better or having a break from these thoughts of worthlessness and failure over the past month?

patient.answer:
A break? No... no, I haven't. Honestly, it's interesting you specifically say 'over the past month,' because that is exactly the timeline we're looking at here. This whole... this entire heavy, crushing feeling, it's been going on for just about a month now. Exactly a month, really. It all started right around the time my daughter left for college out of state. 

We had spent the whole summer getting her ready, you know, buying the extra-long twin sheets and the shower caddies and mapping out the drive. She's going to a school a few states over, about an eight-hour drive depending on traffic, so she was going to be really, truly away from home for the first time. I remember standing out there in the driveway, watching her pull out, just staring at the taillights as she disappeared around the corner at the end of our street. And it was just... it was like a switch flipped right then and there. 

Since that day, for this entire past month, there hasn't been a single break. Not even an hour of feeling slightly better. You'd think, logically, there would be an afternoon where the fog lifts just a little bit, maybe a Tuesday where I don't feel quite so useless or a morning where I can actually focus on a newspaper without the guilt eating at me. But... no. It's been a solid, unbroken month of just sitting in that recliner, looping those same thoughts of failure over and over. Ever since she crossed the state line, it's just been this constant, relentless weight, every single day. No breaks at all.

patient.answer:
Interfering? Yes. Yes, absolutely. It has completely derailed everything. I mean, you know I mentioned that electric bill earlier, but that is really just the tip of the iceberg. There is a stack of mail on the kitchen island that I haven't touched in weeks. It's just sitting there, growing, and I walk past it every day and do nothing. And the house projects... I used to pride myself on keeping this place in top shape. I'm an engineer, right? I fix things. But right now, the deck needs sealing, and there's a leaky faucet in the half-bath downstairs that I actually bought the replacement parts for right before my daughter left for school. Those parts are just sitting on the workbench in the garage. I walk out there, I look at them, and I just... I can't make myself pick up a wrench. I can't make myself follow through on even the most basic, straightforward tasks. It's like there's this massive, invisible wall between me and doing anything productive. 

And it's not just the chores or the house maintenance, either. It's the people. I've completely stopped seeing the few people I used to actually count on. I had this book club I went to—a really sharp group of folks, mostly other retired or semi-retired professionals, and we'd get together and really dig into some heavy non-fiction, history, biographies, that sort of thing. I haven't been to a meeting or even replied to their emails in a month. Same with my riding group. I used to go out on these long weekend bike rides with a couple of guys, just putting in the miles, getting some fresh air. Now, my bike is just hanging from the hooks in the garage, tires probably completely flat by now. I just ignore their texts when they ask where I've been. I can't face them. I have nothing to say to them. 

So, yes, it's interfering with every single aspect of my daily life. And honestly, doctor, I don't feel safe just brushing this off anymore. I really don't. For the first couple of weeks, I tried to tell myself I was just in a funk, you know, just adjusting to the empty nest and I'd snap out of it. But... but like I told you about the other night, when I caught myself organizing my finances, making that meticulous roadmap for my family like someone else was going to need to take over because I wouldn't be here... that was a line crossed. When you can't even manage to pay a simple utility bill or fix a sink, but you can perfectly, methodically plan out your own permanent absence... you can't just ignore that. You can't just pretend it's a passing phase. It has completely taken over my life.

Worse? Yeah... yeah, it's definitely compounding. It's like... well, if you think about a feedback loop in an audio system, right? It starts out as this low, barely noticeable hum, but then the microphone picks it up again, and it feeds back into itself, over and over, until it's just this deafening screech that completely drowns out everything else in the room. That is exactly what is happening in my head right now. 

When it first started a month ago, it was just this quiet, nagging thought. But now... honestly, doctor, that feedback loop is the whole reason I finally made this appointment. I came in because I just can't shake this feeling that I completely failed. I sit there in the living room and look down the hall at her empty bedroom door, and instead of feeling proud that we got her to college, I just think of all the ways I fell short. The school plays I missed because I was working those eighty-hour weeks at the engineering firm, the life lessons I somehow forgot to teach her before she drove off... I just feel like I fundamentally failed as a father. 

And then, you know, I look around at my own house, the deck that's rotting, the mail piling up on the island, the fact that I can't even put a wrench to a leaky pipe anymore, and I realize I've failed as a useful person, too. I used to be someone people relied on to fix things, to solve complex problems. Now I'm just dead weight. And that thought... it just keeps looping in my head. It loops and loops, day in and day out, just reinforcing itself, until I reach this point where I honestly feel like I don't deserve much of a future. It's like my expiration date has passed, my usefulness is completely spent, and the longer I sit with these thoughts, the heavier they get, until there's just no room left for anything else. So, yes, it's absolutely getting worse.

Improve? No... no, I really don't see how they could. I mean, it goes right back to what I was just telling you a second ago. That's the exact reason I'm sitting here in this chair today. I failed as a father when she was growing up, and now that I'm just sitting around the house avoiding my friends and ignoring broken faucets, I've completely failed as a useful person, too.

You can't just un-fail. You can't go back in time and be present for the things you missed, and you can't suddenly become this vibrant, indispensable person when you're just... empty. 

So when you ask if I see a way for things to get better, the honest answer is no. Because that constant loop just grinds down any hope or logic I might have left. It just reinforces that exact conclusion I mentioned—that I really don't deserve much of a future. I mean, what kind of future is there for someone who has outlived their usefulness and botched their most important job? You know, I spent my whole career looking at systems, analyzing structural integrity, figuring out how to repair things that were broken. But I look at myself now, and I just see a system that is completely beyond repair. There's no fixing it. There's no moving forward when you know, deep down in your bones, that you're just taking up space. So no, I don't see any way out of this.

doctor.question: Do you feel like these feelings of worthlessness and failure are interfering with your daily life to the point where you are unable to perform even the simplest tasks?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Even simple things like carrying laundry upstairs or sorting the mail feel like I'm moving through wet cement, no matter how long I've been in bed.

patient.answer:
The simplest tasks... yes. Yes, exactly. I mean, I mentioned the mail earlier, right? That stack on the kitchen island. It's not just that I look at it and think about what a failure I am, though that's certainly part of the loop. It's... it's almost like the worthlessness has turned into a physical weight. It has actually manifested in my body. 

I'll wake up—if you can even call it waking up, since I'm mostly just lying there staring at the drywall—and I'll try to bargain with myself. I'll say, 'Okay, today you are just going to sort the mail. Just put the bills in one pile and throw the flyers in the recycling.' Literally the simplest task in the world. A child could do it. But when I actually try to get up and execute that plan... I just can't. Even simple things like carrying a basket of laundry upstairs, or just standing there sorting through those envelopes, it feels like I'm moving through wet cement. Every single movement takes this monumental, Herculean effort that I just don't possess anymore. 

And the thing that really gets me, from a purely logical standpoint, is that it doesn't make any sense. It happens no matter how long I've been in bed. I could be lying in that bed for twelve, fourteen hours, completely inactive, resting my body, and I still wake up feeling this... this crushing, bone-deep exhaustion. It's like gravity has been dialed up just for me, pulling me down into the floorboards. So when I look at the mail, or I look at that wrench sitting on the workbench... I'm not just fighting the mental block of feeling utterly useless. I'm fighting this sheer, physical inability to push my own limbs through the air. So, yes, the simplest tasks are completely off the table. I just... I don't have the energy to even go through the motions anymore.

doctor.question: Have you ever had a moment in the past month where you felt your worthlessness might be something you could overcome?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can't shake this feeling that I failed as a father and as a useful person, and it keeps looping in my head until I feel like I don't deserve much of a future.

patient.answer:
Overcome it? In the past month? Honestly, doctor... no. Not even for a fleeting second. I know I sound like a broken record here, and I know I keep circling back to the same point, but it really is the crux of this whole thing. Like I said, I came in today, made this appointment and sat in this chair, specifically because I just can't shake this feeling that I failed as a father and as a useful person. 

You ask about overcoming it, and my mind immediately tries to approach it like an engineering problem, right? Because that's what I did for thirty years. You identify the structural weakness, you apply a fix, you test the load, and you move on. But there is no fix for the past. I can't retrofit my daughter's childhood. I can't go back and be the guy who didn't miss her life because he was staring at blueprints. I sit there and try to reason with myself, maybe try to force a moment where I feel like I can overcome it, but then that loop just starts up again. 

It just keeps looping in my head, over and over, drowning out any rational thought or any tiny glimmer of hope that I could somehow redeem myself. It plays this agonizing highlight reel of every mistake, every rotting board on my deck, every time I wasn't there... and it just amplifies it all until I feel like I don't deserve much of a future. I mean, how do you overcome a failure that is already complete? You can't. The concrete is already poured and set. So, no, there hasn't been a single moment where I thought I could beat this. When a conviction is that deep, and when it's constantly echoing in your own mind, you don't overcome it. You just... you just endure it until it wears you down to nothing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's feelings of worthlessness are persistent and unchanging

patient.answer:
Slightly better? Hopeful? No... no, I really haven't. I mean, I think I've made it pretty clear that this isn't something that just ebbs and flows for me. It's not like the weather, where you get a cloudy day and then suddenly the sun peaks through for an afternoon. It's a constant, heavy overcast. It's like I was saying before about the physical weight of it, the way it just pulls me down into the mattress. When you wake up every single day feeling like you're moving through wet cement, and your brain is just playing that same miserable tape on a loop... there really isn't any room for hope to squeeze its way in. 

I try to think back over the last thirty days, you know, just to be thorough, to see if there was maybe one morning where I woke up and thought, 'Hey, maybe today won't be a total write-off.' But I just draw a blank. Every day just blurs into the next. It's just the same routine of waking up exhausted, staring at the ceiling, trying to talk myself into doing something as simple as sorting the mail, failing at that, and then just sitting there feeling like an absolute waste of space. 

And it's hard to feel hopeful when you look around your life and all you see are the things you've neglected or the people you've let down. Like my daughter... I mean, I can't even pick up the phone to call her because what would I even say? 'Hey, sorry I wasn't there when you were a kid, and by the way, I'm currently too tired to even take out the recycling'? There's no hope in that. There's no bright side. It's just a steady, unrelenting decline. So, no, to answer your question, there hasn't been a single moment of feeling better or hopeful.
